2.1.b:
An implant works only if it stops moving on the bone; there are two ways to achieve that.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how is a hip implant fixed to bone?"
- "Two ways: **cement** (grout, not glue) or **biological** fixation."
- "Biological means **ingrowth** into pores or **on-growth** onto a rough surface."
- "Cement fixes in **minutes**; bone fixes a press-fit implant over **weeks to months**."

### Methods of Fixation
Both methods chase the same thing: no motion at the interface.

#### Definition
- **Implant fixation** couples the component to bone, so the interface does not move
[[FIG: Fig 2.1 · 2.1
- **Cement** gives full fixation in theatre
- **Biological** fixation is press-fit now, permanent once bone grows in

#### Primary and Secondary Stability
- Primary stability comes from the **press-fit**; secondary from **osseointegration**
- Together they decide weight bearing, and early versus late failure

#### Hybrid Fixation
| Combination | Cup | Stem |
|---|---|---|
| **Hybrid** | cementless | cemented |
| **Reverse hybrid** | cemented | cementless |

- A porous-coated cementless cup is preferred; cement the cup in the elderly or poor bone stock

### Cemented Fixation
Cement does not stick to bone; it locks into it.

#### Microinterlock
- **PMMA** (polymethyl methacrylate) is **grout, not glue**: it interlocks with trabecular bone
[[FIG: Fig 2.2 · 2.1
- It gives macro- and micro-interlock, so load reaches bone more evenly
- The **mantle** then transfers load to bone, purely mechanically
- Both surfaces need preparing: bone cleaned of blood and debris, and a stem of one philosophy
- So **clean, dry bone** gives deeper interdigitation

#### Weak Points
- Cement works in dense and in porous bone
- It is weakest at its **interfaces** (cement–bone, stem–cement), not in the bulk

MEMORY HOOK — grout between tiles
- Cement is tile grout, not glue: it holds by filling every gap, so keep the bone clean and dry.

#### Barrack Grading of the Cement Mantle
The **Barrack & Harris** grade scores the femoral mantle on the post-operative film.

| Grade (Campbell) | Post-operative radiograph |
|---|---|
| **A** | complete filling: **white-out** |
| **B** | radiolucency ≤50% of the cement–bone interface |
| **C** | radiolucency 50–99%, or an incomplete mantle |
| **D** | 100% radiolucency, or **no cement below the stem tip** |

- Cup zones: DeLee–Charnley, lateral to medial; stem: Gruen 1–7 on AP, 8–14 on lateral
- Zones → 06 Post-op radiograph · loosening signs → 11 Painful arthroplasty

### Biological Fixation
Without cement, bone itself must grip the metal, either into it or onto it.

#### Ingrowth
- In **ingrowth**, endosteal bone grows **through pores**, like a healing cancellous defect
[[FIG: Fig 2.3 · 2.1
- The pores sit only in the **external coating**, so the solid stem carries the load
- Beads are sintered at high temperature, which can lower the implant's fatigue strength
- Fibre mesh is diffusion-bonded; porous tantalum resembles trabecular bone

#### On-growth
- In **on-growth**, bone grows **onto** micro-divots made by **grit blasting** or **plasma spray**
[[FIG: Fig 2.4 · 2.1
- Grit blasting uses aluminium oxide
- On-growth needs a **double-wedge taper** and a **press-fit**
- Grit-blasted stems are usually **extensively coated**, to add grip

| Ingrowth — porous coatings | On-growth — rough surfaces |
|---|---|
| **Sintered beads**, most popular (Ti or CoCr) | **grit-blasted** |
| **Ti fibre mesh** · plasma-sprayed Ti alloy | **plasma-sprayed** |
| **Porous tantalum** · Ti foams | — |

#### Cup Coatings and Surface Roughness
- On cups, the commonest coating is **plasma-sprayed Ti particles**; roughness alone is no longer used
- **Ra** (average peak-to-valley) measures roughness: higher means better grip

#### Hydroxyapatite
- **HA** (hydroxyapatite) coats porous or grit-blasted surfaces and speeds bone apposition
[[FIG: Fig 2.5 · 2.1
- Osteoblasts adhere to HA and grow toward bone
- HA closes the gap **from both sides**, so the component migrates less

PITFALL — ingrowth or on-growth?
- Ingrowth goes **into the pores** of a coating; on-growth goes **onto** a rough, non-porous surface
- Say → "Porous coating gives **ingrowth**; grit blast or plasma spray gives **on-growth**; HA speeds both."

2.2.b:
Knowing the two methods, the next question is which one this patient's bone can carry.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you choose cemented or cementless?"
- "Cement needs no biology: **osteoporotic, irradiated, Dorr C** bone, elderly, low demand."
- "Biological needs **living bone** and a matching canal: young, active, **Dorr A or B**."
- "The cup is almost always **cementless**, because cement fails in **shear**."

### Bone Quality
Biological fixation needs living, healthy bone; cement does not.

#### The Femoral Component
- Cement fills voids in any bone, so it is the fallback in poor bone
- Biological fixation is defeated by **osteopenia, infection, tumour, radiation**
- Cement the stem in osteoporotic, irradiated, **Dorr C** or deformed femora

#### Fracture Risk and the Acetabular Component
- Elderly neck fractures and Dorr C women: a **cemented** stem means fewer periprosthetic fractures (Campbell)
- The **cementless cup** is the rule, in the young and in older patients with good bone
- In poor bone, impaction may break it, so cement it
- Prior **pelvic radiotherapy** means poor ingrowth and early loosening: the classic cementless trap

#### Indications at a Glance
| Cemented | Cementless |
|---|---|
| rheumatological disease | very young |
| older, **low activity** | good bone stock |
| osteoporotic bone | **Dorr A** |
| **Dorr C** | all acetabular components |

### Clinical Cases
The same rules, applied to real patients, give opposite answers.

#### Same Disease, Opposite Fixation
| Patient (Prof Sherif Khaled) | Fixation | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **SLE** (systemic lupus), 36 years, osteoporosis | **cemented cup and stem** | fear of losing a cementless cup |
| **JRA** (juvenile rheumatoid arthritis), 16, wheelchair-bound | **cemented** | poor bone |
| **RA** (rheumatoid arthritis), 30, good bone, suitable Dorr type | **cementless** | bone allows it |
[[FIG: Fig 2.6–2.7 · 2.2

#### Young Patients
- At 38, a previously **nailed femur** had a disrupted canal and thin cortex
[[FIG: Fig 2.8 · 2.2
- So a **prophylactic cerclage** was added, and the stem cemented: easier, standard stem, cheaper
- Cementless would need a distal **modular revision stem** (Reef, Revitan), with more stress shielding
- Today most would choose a cementless cup and stem
- At 46, post-acetabular-fracture AVN left a small superolateral defect
[[FIG: Fig 2.9 · 2.2
- It took a femoral head **graft with two screws** under a cementless cup
- Dorr A bone, so the stem was cementless too
- Modular stems and dual mobility have no role in a routine primary

#### Older Patients
| Patient | Fixation |
|---|---|
| 62 years, OA, Dorr C | cemented cup and stem · **loaded taper** preferred |
| 60-year-old woman, OA | **hybrid**: cementless cup, cemented stem |
| 75 years, neck fracture | **cemented bipolar** |
[[FIG: Fig 2.10 · 2.2

### Failure of Cemented Acetabular Components
Cement is strong in one direction only, and the cup loads it in the wrong ones.

#### Loading of the Cement
- Cement is strong in **compression**, moderate in **shear**, poor in **tension**
- The stem loads it in **compression**
- A cup at 30–50° loads it in **shear and tension**, so voids form and it fails

#### Composite Action
- **Composite action**: concrete takes compression, steel rods take tension and shear
[[FIG: Fig 2.11 · 2.2
- Hence a **cementless acetabulum**, and the **hybrid hip**

PITFALL — "cement is strong, so cement the cup"?
- Cement fails in **shear**, and a cup at 30–50° loads it in shear and tension
- Say → "Cement the **stem**, which works in compression; the cup is **cementless** unless bone is poor."

#### Outcomes and the Registry Debate
- **Cementless cup** survival: **96%** at 10 years, ≈**90%** at 20 (Prof Kamal)
- A 2013 study of ≈27,000 hips found **no difference** for older designs
- Its designs are old, so **technique** remains the key point
- The **English National Joint Registry** trends to cement; England cements at any age, even 14
- UK surgeons are cement-trained; few Americans are, so both literatures are biased

### Dorr Classification
Bone quality is half the question; the canal's shape is the other half.

#### Shape of the Canal
- **Cement** fits any canal, even a **stovepipe**; **cementless** needs stem–endosteal contact
- The ideal is a **champagne-flute** canal, which grips a tapered stem

#### Calcar-to-Canal Ratio
- **Calcar-to-canal ratio** = canal width 10 cm below ÷ width at mid-lesser trochanter (Prof Fahmy)
[[FIG: Fig 2.12 · 2.2
- A high ratio means thin cortices: little to wedge, so cement is safer
- Template on **AP and lateral**: a funnel on the AP may be a stovepipe on the lateral

| Dorr | Ratio | Films (AP + lateral) | Stem |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** champagne flute | <0.5 | thick cortices on both views | cementless · young, active |
| **B** intermediate, mild cortical flaring | 0.5–0.75 | posterior cortex thin on lateral | either: surgeon's choice |
| **C** stovepipe | >0.75 | thin cortices on both views | cemented · elderly |

#### Zones of Fixation
- The zone of fixation is the metaphysis in A, metaphyseal–diaphyseal in B
[[FIG: Fig 2.13 · 2.2
- In C it is the diaphysis, because the metaphysis is lost
- A cementless stem in Dorr C brings **undersizing, subsidence**, and fracture if a fit is forced

MEMORY HOOK — the cork and the chimney
- Dorr **A**, a champagne flute, grips a stem like a cork; Dorr **C**, a stovepipe, is a chimney: cement it.

### Spotorno Index
Dorr reads the canal alone; Spotorno adds the patient and gives a score.

#### Scoring
| Item (Handbook) | Finding → points |
|---|---|
| **MCI** (morphological cortical index) = outer diameter at lesser trochanter ÷ canal 7 cm below | >3 → 0 · 2.7–3.0 → 1 · 2.3–2.6 → 2 · <2.3 → 4 |
| **Sex** | male 0 · female 1 |
| **Age** | <50 → 0 · 50–60 → 1 · 60–70 → 2 · >70 → 3 |
| **Singh index** | grade 6 → 0 · 5 → 1 · 3–4 → 2 · 1–2 → 4 |

- The total decides: **≤4 cementless · 5 discuss · ≥6 cemented**
- Bone items score up to 4 each, so they can outweigh age and sex
- It guides the **stem** only; the cup is decided separately

#### Singh Index
- Singh grades how the trabecular groups of the proximal femur vanish
[[FIG: Fig 2.14 · 2.2
- The secondary groups go first, the principal compressive group last

### Khanuja Classification
Once cementless is chosen, the stem's shape decides where it grips.

#### Basis of the Classification
- Khanuja sorted every market stem by where it was designed to fix: 4 main, 2 extra types
[[FIG: Fig 2.15 · 2.2
- Outcome depends more on stem **geometry** than on material or surface

| Type (Prof Hazem) | Shape | Grips |
|---|---|---|
| **1** single wedge | broad in one plane, thin in the other | metaphysis |
| **2** double wedge | metaphyseal filling · removes much good bone | metaphysis |
| **3A** | round cone · three-point fixation · most of the market | metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction |
| **3B** Wagner | splined cone | junction and proximal diaphysis |
| **3C** | rectangle, fully coated · four-point fixation | metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction |
| **4** | cylindrical, fully coated · diaphyseal **scratch fit** · proximal collar | diaphysis |
| **5** modular · **6** anatomical | separate sleeve and stem · curved | both · metaphysis |

#### Types 1 and 2: Metaphyseal Fixation
- **Type 1** is a flat wedge, so it depends on **correct positioning**
[[FIG: Fig 2.16 · 2.2
- **Type 2** fills the metaphysis in both planes: impossible in Dorr A, works in Dorr C
[[FIG: Fig 2.17–2.18 · 2.2
- It removes much good bone and is hard through a minimally invasive approach

#### Type 3: Metaphyseal–Diaphyseal Fixation
- **Type 3** is the stem **most surgeons** use: straight, with a continuous taper
[[FIG: Fig 2.19 · 2.2
- It was designed for Dorr B, but works in Dorr C too
- **3A** is conical, not cylindrical, coated on its proximal two-thirds: the simplest to use
- **3B Wagner**: splines resist rotation, and the cone allows any version, for deformed femora
[[FIG: Fig 2.20 · 2.2
- **3C**: the rectangle grips four corners on AP and three points on lateral
[[FIG: Fig 2.21 · 2.2

#### Types 4 to 6
- **Type 4** scratch fit cracks the diaphysis, so its use has declined
- Its proximal **collar** adds proximal loading and axial stability
- **Type 5** is modular: metaphysis and diaphysis sized separately, e.g. S-ROM
[[FIG: Fig 2.22 · 2.2
- Its distal part fixes by screws or coating; the proximal part grips the metaphysis
- **Type 6** is anatomical: wide laterally and posteriorly, curved to the proximal femur
[[FIG: Fig 2.23 · 2.2
- It comes as right and left stems that match anteversion, and is back on the market

#### Short Stems
- A **short stem** is ≈half a 14 cm stem, metaphyseal only
[[FIG: Fig 2.24 · 2.2
- By neck kept: collum (whole neck), partial collum, trochanter-sparing, trochanter-harming

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Khanuja (2011): the fixation area grows with the type — metaphysis (1–2), junction (3), diaphysis (4)**

### Fixation Time and Weight Bearing
The method also sets how soon the patient may load the leg.

#### Timing
- Cement fixes in **minutes**, so cemented hips bear **immediate full** weight: good for the frail
- Biological fixation takes **weeks to months**, so classically weight bearing is **protected**

#### Protected Weight Bearing
- Modern press-fit often allows early full weight bearing
- But **protect** it if press-fit is doubtful: a **calcar crack**, or poor bone

2.3.b:
Cement is the first method; here is what it is made of and how it sets.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is bone cement made of?"
- "Powder: PMMA plus **benzoyl peroxide** initiator. Liquid: **monomer** plus **DMPT** activator."
- "Mixing starts an **exothermic** polymerisation: 80–86 °C in vitro, ≈40–47 °C in the body."
- "Insert in the **working phase**; add antibiotic only as a **heat-stable** powder."

### Composition
Two packs are kept apart until mixing, so nothing sets on the shelf.
[[FIG: Fig 2.25 · 2.3

#### Two Components
- Liquid monomer alone sets slowly, with big heat and **shrinkage**
- Hence most of the polymer comes **pre-polymerised** as powder

#### Powder and Liquid
| Powder | Agent | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Polymer | **PMMA** | scaffold |
| Initiator | **benzoyl peroxide** | free radicals |
| Radiopacifier | **barium sulfate** or zirconium dioxide | visible on X-ray |
| Antibiotic, optional | heat-stable **gentamicin**, tobramycin, vancomycin | local prophylaxis |

| Liquid | Agent | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Monomer | **methyl methacrylate** | polymerises |
| Activator = accelerator | **DMPT** (dimethyl-p-toluidine) | splits benzoyl peroxide at room temperature |
| Inhibitor | **hydroquinone** | shelf life |
| Colorant | chlorophyll (green) · methylene blue | shows excess cement |

MEMORY HOOK — the match and the striker
- The powder carries the match (**benzoyl peroxide**); the liquid carries the striker (**DMPT**) that lights it at room temperature.

### Polymerisation and Heat
Polymerisation gives off heat, but the body cools it.

#### Exothermic Reaction
- Free radicals from initiator and activator break the monomer's carbon double bond
- The reaction is **exothermic**: 80–86 °C in vitro (Prof Fahmy)
[[FIG: Fig 2.26 · 2.3
- In vivo only **40–47 °C**: a thin layer, the stem, blood flow and water cool it
- Thick cement masses get hottest

#### Staff Protection
- The monomer is volatile and irritant, so **closed vacuum mixing** protects staff

### Antibiotic-Loaded Cement
Antibiotic powder can ride in the cement, but every gram costs strength.
- It must be **heat-stable**, water-soluble powder: it survives the heat, then leaches out
- Vancomycin and gentamicin are used most, because they resist the heat
- More powder means weaker cement: **delivery versus strength**
- Commercial packs carry **<1 g** per 40 g, so a spacer needs added drug

PITFALL — how much antibiotic per 40 g of cement?
- Fixation **≤1 g** (Miller) · spacer **3–4 g** · Campbell: 2–4 g vancomycin ± 1.2 g tobramycin
- Handbook ceiling: ≤3–4 g per 40 g of powder
- Say → "**≤1 g to fix · ≤4 g (<10%) in a spacer · never >8 g**" (Prof Abdel Moneim)

### Working Phases
The surgeon has one window, and the clock runs from mixing.

#### Definitions
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Dough time** | from mixing until it no longer sticks to gloves |
| **Working time** | from dough to hardened: the stem goes in |
| **Setting time** | from mixing to hardening = **dough + working time** |
| Low viscosity | long dough, short working: sets fast |
| High viscosity | short dough, long working: sets slowly |

#### Timing in Theatre
- Warmth (theatre or components) shortens all phases; cold lengthens them
- Simplex reaches dough ≈**4 minutes** after mixing; humidity and a warmed stem change it (Campbell)
- Insert in the **working phase**: stiff enough to resist bleeding, fluid enough to interdigitate
- Too fluid or chilled cement runs out of the canal, so pressurisation fails
- Stem proud after an early set: accept it, or remove all cement and redo; **never hammer**

### Mechanical Properties
Cement is brittle, and that explains every way it fails.

#### Short-Term Properties
- The interface is **static and brittle**: cracks never repair, and failure is abrupt
[[FIG: Fig 2.27 · 2.3
- Cement is **notch-sensitive**: a notch is a **stress riser**, so at revision crack it first

#### Creep, Stress Relaxation and Fatigue
- Over years: **creep**, **stress relaxation** and **fatigue failure**
- Creep: cement in a serrated metal cone takes the imprint only when loaded
- Fatigue strikes below ultimate strength, under cyclic load, at high-stress points
- Stress relaxation protects against it

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "describe modern cementing technique"
- "Third generation: **pulsed lavage**, brush, dry, **plug**, **vacuum mixing**, **gun**, **pressuriser**, centralisers."
- "The aim is a uniform mantle **>2 mm**, no voids, and a central stem."
- "Two stems: **composite beam** (bonded) or **taper-slip** (polished, subsides). Never mix them."

### Cementing Generations
Each generation fixed a failure of the one before.

#### Features by Generation
| Generation | Canal | Mixing · delivery | Centralisation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1st** | rasps, suction, gauze · femoral-head bone plug or none | hand · **finger packing** | distal only |
| **2nd** | brush, sponge, pre-made **plug** | hand · retrograde **cement gun** | proximal + distal |
| **3rd** | **pulsed lavage**, brush, drying | **vacuum** or centrifuge · gun + **pressuriser**, rubber seal | proximal + distal |
| **4th**, some texts | as 3rd | as 3rd | + precoated or roughened stem |

#### Rationale
- The 1st generation had no preparation, plug or pressure, so blood and voids were trapped
[[FIG: Fig 2.28 · 2.4
- Air bubbles start cracks
- An off-centre stem leaves a thin mantle, which cracks first
- Recent advances aim to shorten mixing time

#### Cement Restrictor and Stem Position
- Place the **restrictor** ≈**1–2 cm** below the stem tip, so the mantle passes the tip (Campbell)
- A **varus** stem thins the mantle **proximal-medially** and **distal-laterally**

### Factors Affecting Cement Fixation
Most failures trace back to contamination, porosity or mechanics.

| Weakens | Strengthens |
|---|---|
| time (static interface) · moisture | good design · **centralisation** |
| blood, tissue inclusions | **vacuum or centrifuge mixing**: no air voids |
| excess additives: antibiotic, barium | **pressurisation**: compaction |
| stem moved while setting · high-speed mixing | — |
| thin mantle · low temperature (Handbook) | — |

- Moving the stem breaks the cement–stem bond and leaves it rotated after hardening

### The Cement Mantle
The mantle is the product of all this work, so it has target numbers.

#### Target Thickness
- Aim **>2 mm**, uniform, low porosity, pressurised, on clean dry bone (Prof Fahmy)
- Use a stiff stem with no sharp edges, held still while it sets
- The stem fills ≈**80%** of the canal's cross-section
- The ideal femoral mantle is ≈**4 mm proximally**, **2 mm distally** (Campbell)

#### Mantle Stresses
- The mantle is in compression; the cement–metal interface takes **shear and tension**
[[FIG: Fig 2.29 · 2.4
- Voids weaken it
- Failure starts at the stem–cement interface: debonding first, then cement fracture
- Cobalt-chrome is favoured: its higher modulus lowers proximal mantle stress

#### Cemented Acetabular Component
- PMMA spacers **3 mm** high give a mantle of ≈**3 mm** (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 2.30 · 2.4
- The course gives 2–4 mm, ≈2.5 mm (Prof Kamal); at least 2 mm (Handbook)
- Outer **grooves** give macro-interlock with the cement
[[FIG: Fig 2.31 · 2.4
- A **marker wire** shows cup position and wear on films
- It also shows the cement mantle's thickness around the cup

### Composite Beam and Loaded Taper
With the mantle made, the stem's design decides how it lives inside it.

#### Comparison
Both philosophies come from engineering: a rod inside another material.

| | **Composite beam** = shape-closed | **Loaded taper** = taper-slip, force-closed |
|---|---|---|
| Surface · shape | rough · anatomical | **polished** · tapered in two planes · void at tip |
| Collar | favoured: transmits load, less proximal shielding | harmful: blocks subsidence |
| Concept | **bonded** to cement: initial stability | **subsides** ≈1 mm in year 1: secondary stability |
| A void | harmful: allows subsidence, so cracks | needed below the tip |
| Forgiveness | not forgiving: any micromotion cracks it | more forgiving |
| Example | — | **Exeter** |

#### Composite Beam
- A composite beam must never move: once micromotion starts, the cement cracks
[[FIG: Fig 2.32–2.33 · 2.4
- Stem, cement and bone share the load, and stress gathers distally

#### Loaded Taper
- Cement settles in year 1; engineers used that motion for secondary stability
- Ling's design is collarless, polished and double-tapered; registries show slightly less loosening
- A loaded taper goes in with a **hollow centraliser** at the tip
- Its **controlled subsidence** tightens the wedge in its mantle
[[FIG: Fig 2.34 · 2.4

#### Mechanism of Subsidence
- Subsidence puts **radial compression** in cement and tensile **hoop stress** in bone (Prof Fahmy)
[[FIG: Fig 2.35 · 2.4
- The taper turns shear into radial compression, top to bottom, so less proximal shielding
[[FIG: Fig 2.36 · 2.4
- A barrel works alike: its steel hoops turn the load into hoop stress
[[FIG: Fig 2.37 · 2.4
- **Creep** increases interdigitation; **stress relaxation** dissipates bone tension at rest

MEMORY HOOK — the marriage and the wedge
- A composite beam is a marriage: one crack ends it. A taper-slip is a wedge: it sinks ≈1 mm and tightens.

PITFALL — a collar on a polished taper?
- A **collar** on a polished taper blocks subsidence, so it is harmful
- It sinks ≈1 mm in year 1; Prof Sherif Khaled accepts **1–2 mm** (→ 14)
- Campbell gives no number, only "a small amount"
- Say → "Polished, collarless, tapered = loaded taper; rough, collared = composite beam. Never mix them."

### Cementing in Total Knee Arthroplasty
In the knee, cement is the standard; the steps differ from the hip.

#### Fixation
- Cement gives more reliable long-term fixation; cementless knees were revised **1.4×** more (Campbell)
- Early, sticky cement intrudes **2–5 mm** into cancellous bone: enough for life (Campbell)
- A cemented keel equals an extended press-fit stem

#### Patella and Defects
- A patella under **12–13 mm** is not resurfaced: it breaks through the peg holes
- Small contained tibial defects take cement; larger ones a graft with two screws (→ 14)
- The operative steps of cementing a TKA → 08 TKA technique (Cementing)

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what does bone ingrowth need?"
- "Living bone, pores of **50–400 µm**, a gap **<50 µm**, a still surface."
- "Micromotion under **50 µm**: bone grows in; over **150 µm**: fibrous tissue."
- "Enhance it with coating, **press-fit** or screws, at some cost to bone."

### Determinants of Bone Ingrowth
Like fracture healing, ingrowth needs living bone, a scaffold, a small gap and **stability**.

#### Implant and Surgeon Factors
| Factor | Target |
|---|---|
| Pore size · depth | **50–400 µm** (Prof Fahmy) · 100–400 µm (Campbell) · deeper = more penetration |
| Porosity | **40–50%** best |
| Gap to bone | **<50 µm** |
| Micromotion | bone **<50 µm** · fibrous tissue **>150 µm** (Miller) |
| Bone | viable · irradiation leads to aseptic loosening |

#### Surgical Technique
- Ream so the implant rests on **cortical**, not cancellous bone
- If the implant rotates, the gap widens and fixation fails
- **Initial rigid fixation** is critical: a failure means stability or contact was missing
- Stable fibrous versus loose stem → 11 Painful arthroplasty

MEMORY HOOK — shy bone
- Bone is shy: it moves in only if the surface stays still (**<50 µm**); over **150 µm**, fibrous tissue moves in.

### Enhancement of Biological Fixation
Porous ingrowth beats grit-blasted on-growth, so the aim is to strengthen on-growth.

#### Strategies
- It needs **immediate mechanical stability** and intimate bone contact
[[FIG: Fig 2.38 · 2.5
- Bone grows only on a **still** surface, so early micromotion must fall

| Strategy | How |
|---|---|
| 1 · More surface | extensive coating |
| 2 · Initial stability | **press-fit** rather than line-to-line |
| 3 · Extra hold | **screws** for grit-blasted cups |

- But strategies 1 and 2 also raised fracture risk: stability versus bone damage

#### Press-Fit and Line-to-Line Fixation
- **Press-fit**: under-reamed, so the rim is compressed and the cup needs no screws
[[FIG: Fig 2.39 · 2.5
- **Line-to-line**: the cup needs screws, and the stem is extensively coated for a frictional fit
- Add screws if bone contact is poor, or the cup does not press-fit on hammering
- **Press-fit is better** than line-to-line

#### Under-Reaming
- Under-ream the rim by **1–2 mm**; if the fit is poor, add **screws**
- Too much under-reaming brings **acetabular fracture** or a dome gap
- So check seating through the **apical hole**

2.6.t: Advantages and Disadvantages of Each Method
2.6.b:
With both methods known, set them side by side.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "cemented or cementless — pros and cons?"
- "Cement: any bone or canal, **immediate**, cheaper; but **brittle**, with **BCIS** risk."
- "Biological: a **living interface** that repairs itself; needs good bone."
- "Its price: **stress shielding** and **periprosthetic fracture**."

### Cemented Fixation
Cement wins where biology is poor or time is short.

#### Advantages
- It is easier, uses a standard stem, and is **cheaper**; it can also carry antibiotic
- Stem survival is **97%** at 10 years, **89%** at 15 (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- It suits rheumatological disease and the old, inactive patient

#### Cement as a Tumour Adjuvant
- After curettage of a giant cell tumour, PMMA fills the cavity and its heat kills residual cells

#### Local and Systemic Complications
- Locally, **thermal injury** and necrosis; **cemented cups** also fail often
- Pressurisation pushes marrow and fat **emboli**; the monomer causes **vasodilation**
- So hypotension, hypoxia, bradycardia, even arrest can follow

#### Bone Cement Implantation Syndrome
- **BCIS** (bone cement implantation syndrome) threatens frail fracture patients most, so warn the anaesthetist
- Prevent it with **lavage**, canal **venting** and haemodynamic monitoring

MEMORY HOOK — the piston in the marrow
- Pressurised cement is a piston in a marrow tube: fat goes to the lungs, so warn the anaesthetist.

### Biological Fixation
Bone that grows in can mend itself, which cement never can.

#### Advantages
- The **dynamic** interface lets new bone repair minor defects
- At age **15**, go cementless
[[FIG: Fig 2.40 · 2.6
- Cement the young only if trained in good technique, as in the UK

#### Load Transfer and Stress Shielding
- **Proximal coating** loads the metaphysis and proximal diaphysis; **extensive** coating loads the diaphysis
[[FIG: Fig 2.41 · 2.6
- So extensive coating brings proximal **stress shielding** (mechanism → 01 Bearings)
- Stem stiffness rises with the **fourth power** of its diameter (Campbell)
- So large stems shield more and cause thigh pain

#### Periprosthetic Fracture
- **Periprosthetic fracture** is commoner with press-fit and extensive coating
- A cemented stem goes in a size below the last broach; cementless goes line-to-line or larger
- A **calcar crack** on broaching calls for a prophylactic **cerclage wire**
- Spot welds, load bypass and Engh grades → 11 Painful arthroplasty

#### Radiographic Signs of Fixation
| Well-fixed cementless stem (Prof Fahmy) | Well-fixed cementless cup |
|---|---|
| **spot welds** near the coating's end | intact screws |
| proximal stress shielding | no progressive radiolucent lines |
| no radiolucent lines | no migration on serial films |
| no subsidence on serial films | — |

- On a film, read shielding, calcar resorption, spot welds and any pedestal
[[FIG: Fig 2.42 · 2.6

#### Cement as a Tumour Adjuvant
- After curettage of a giant cell tumour, PMMA fills the cavity and its heat kills residual cells

#### Local and Systemic Complications
- Locally, **thermal injury** and necrosis; **cemented cups** also fail often
- Pressurisation pushes marrow and fat **emboli**; the monomer causes **vasodilation**
- So hypotension, hypoxia, bradycardia, even arrest can follow

#### Bone Cement Implantation Syndrome
- **BCIS** (bone cement implantation syndrome) threatens frail fracture patients most, so warn the anaesthetist
- Prevent it with **lavage**, canal **venting** and haemodynamic monitoring

MEMORY HOOK — the piston in the marrow
- Pressurised cement is a piston in a marrow tube: fat goes to the lungs, so warn the anaesthetist.

2.6.2.b:
Bone that grows in can mend itself, which cement never can.

#### Advantages
- The **dynamic** interface lets new bone repair minor defects
- At age **15**, go cementless
[[FIG: Fig 2.40 · 2.6
- Cement the young only if trained in good technique, as in the UK

#### Load Transfer and Stress Shielding
- **Proximal coating** loads the metaphysis and proximal diaphysis; **extensive** coating loads the diaphysis
[[FIG: Fig 2.41 · 2.6
- So extensive coating brings proximal **stress shielding** (mechanism → 01 Bearings)
- Stem stiffness rises with the **fourth power** of its diameter (Campbell)
- So large stems shield more and cause thigh pain

#### Periprosthetic Fracture
- **Periprosthetic fracture** is commoner with press-fit and extensive coating
- A cemented stem goes in a size below the last broach; cementless goes line-to-line or larger
- A **calcar crack** on broaching calls for a prophylactic **cerclage wire**
- Spot welds, load bypass and Engh grades → 11 Painful arthroplasty

#### Radiographic Signs of Fixation
| Well-fixed cementless stem (Prof Fahmy) | Well-fixed cementless cup |
|---|---|
| **spot welds** near the coating's end | intact screws |
| proximal stress shielding | no progressive radiolucent lines |
| no radiolucent lines | no migration on serial films |
| no subsidence on serial films | — |

- On a film, read shielding, calcar resorption, spot welds and any pedestal

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "where do you put acetabular screws?"
- "Only for poor press-fit, fracture or revision; they need a **modular** shell."
- "**Wasielewski quadrants**: a line from ASIS through the acetabular centre, plus a perpendicular."
- "**Posterosuperior** is safe, posteroinferior ≤20 mm; avoid the **anterior** quadrants."

### Indications and Drawbacks
Screws are a tool for a weak fixation, not a routine.

#### Indications
- Use them for poor fixation, a **periprosthetic fracture**, or a **revision**
- They need a **modular** shell; a **monoblock** cup takes no screws (figure → 04)

#### Drawbacks
- Each screw is a debris path: **wear particles**, fretting corrosion, neurovascular injury
- Close unused holes with **hole eliminators**, so less debris reaches the pelvis

### Wasielewski Quadrant System
Two lines divide the socket into four zones of risk.

#### Reference Lines
- **Line A**: **ASIS** (anterior superior iliac spine) through the acetabular centre to the posterior fovea
[[FIG: Fig 2.43 · 2.7
- **Line B**: perpendicular to line A at the centre, making four quadrants
- The course variant: an ASIS–ischium line plus a perpendicular; screws only in its posterosuperior part

#### Zones of Risk
| Zone | Quadrant | At risk · rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Safe** | posterosuperior | sciatic nerve, superior gluteal nerve and vessels · strong bone: screws **>25 mm** (Campbell) |
| **Caution** | posteroinferior | sciatic nerve, inferior gluteal and pudendal vessels · bone ≈25 mm: screws ≤**20 mm** (Prof Khaled Fawzy) |
| **Danger** | anteroinferior | obturator nerve and vessels |
| **Death** | anterosuperior | **external iliac** artery and vein |

- The posterosuperior nerve and vessels lie just below the zone, under ≈25 mm of gluteal muscle (Handbook)

#### Altered Anatomy
- Abnormal version or a **high hip centre** shifts the quadrants
- Then only the peripheral posterior halves are safe

MEMORY HOOK — guests use the back door
- Screws are polite guests: they use the back door (**posterosuperior**); the front-top door opens onto the external iliac.

#### Vascular Anatomy
- The anterior vessels lie on the inner wall with no soft-tissue cover, so injury may show late
[[FIG: Fig 2.44 · 2.7
- The **corona mortis** joins obturator and external iliac or epigastric vessels over the ramus
- Its injury causes catastrophic bleeding

#### Safe Technique
- Use a depth gauge and a hand-controlled drill, and feel the far cortex
- Prefer posterosuperior holes

PITFALL — "Bozic quadrants"?
- The Handbook says "Bozic", line ASIS → ischium; Campbell says **Wasielewski**, line ASIS → acetabular centre
- Say → "**Wasielewski**: ASIS through the acetabular centre, perpendicular at the centre · posterosuperior is safe."
